THE PITCH

A $34,000 letter lands in a parent's mailbox. The adult daughter opens it. SSA says a mistake from years ago means half the monthly check stops in 30 days. She calls attorneys. One after another says no, there is no good outcome in it for them. She calls SSA. She gets a different answer every call. SSA sent roughly 2 million of these notices last year, and since April 25, 2025, every new Title II notice defaults to 50 percent withholding, five times the 10 percent cap most families faced in 2024.

WHO IT'S FOR

WHY NOW

SSA switched to 50% default withholding on April 25, 2025, and the panic has not gone away

On April 25, 2025, SSA issued Emergency Message 25029. Every new Title II overpayment notice (retirement, SSDI, survivors) now defaults to 50% withholding of the monthly check, up from the 10% cap that applied for most of 2024. If the beneficiary does nothing for about 90 days, SSA starts taking half the check automatically. SSI stayed at 10%. This is a 5x jump in the per-household dollar pain of a single notice, on a check that is often the person's only income.

The volume underneath that policy is already huge. SSA sends roughly 2 million overpayment notices a year across its programs and had $23 billion in uncollected overpayments on the books as of September 2023. SSA actuaries estimate the higher recovery rate will pull in an extra $7 billion over 10 years, which is a plain statement that the agency plans to issue and enforce more notices, not fewer. At the same time, SSA announced in February 2025 it would cut staff from about 57,000 to 50,000, from a workforce already near a 50-year low. Fewer humans processing more notices is a well-known recipe for more errors, longer phone holds, and more families stuck filing SSA-632 waivers with no one to call.

newLayoutSections.Who You're Up Against:
8 PLAYERS

24help.org

(Dr.

Allsup

The oldest and largest non-attorney SSDI representation company (founded 1984, 42+ years), has secured $18B in SSDI/Medicare benefits for 220,000+ customers, and runs Seamless ORS (Overpayment Reimbursement Service), but its overpayment product serves LTD insurance carriers and employers recovering money from the beneficiary, not families fighting SSA clawbacks.

Binder & Binder

Binder & Binder, the largest non-attorney SSDI advocate corporation, prepared for bankruptcy in 2014-2015 citing $40M in debt, shrinking demand, and greater government scrutiny; it has since relaunched but focuses only on SSDI benefits claims, not overpayment waivers.

DisabilitySecrets (Nolo)

INCUMBENT

Private disability attorneys who do take SSA overpayment cases typically require a $3,000 retainer up front (15 hours at $200/hour) with no contingency option, because SSA fee-petition rules do not permit the usual 25% back-pay cut on overpayment waivers; this prices out most SSA beneficiaries by design.

Illinois Legal Aid Online

State legal aid clinics (Illinois Legal Aid, Pine Tree Legal Assistance, Legal Aid DC, LawHelpNC, Legal Services Vermont, Disability Rights California, South Carolina Legal Services, Legal Aid NY) publish free SSA-632 waiver guides and sometimes represent clients, but every one gates service by income eligibility and local jurisdiction.

JustAnswer

Runs a paid Social Security Q&A product that routes overpayment panic queries ("Is there a way to stop Social Security from taking $9,089.20 overpayment from my daughter's SSDI benefits?") to on-call experts who point users to Form SSA-632-BK, but it is advice, not done-for-you filing.

Social Security Administration

SSA itself provides free DIY tooling: SSA-632-BK form download, online upload portal through the my Social Security account, and a 1-800-772-1213 phone line that will quick-waive overpayments of $2,000 or less without the form; for larger cases it offers no form-filling help beyond "we will help you fill out the form if you want."

Allsup

The oldest and largest non-attorney SSDI representation company (founded 1984, 42+ years), has secured SSDI benefits for 425,000+ customers with a 97% success rate for those who complete the process, and runs Seamless ORS (Overpayment Reimbursement Services) for insurance carriers, not for families fighting SSA.

newLayoutSections.The Verdict:
Should you build this?

REASONS TO BUILD

The policy clock is on your side: SSA switched to 50% default withholding on April 25, 2025, which means every new notice issued since is five times more painful than it was in 2024.
The attorney door is provably closed: a vision-impaired mom with a $34K overpayment wrote that no attorney would help, and SSA fee rules structurally prevent contingency work on waivers, so there is no incumbent fighting for your lane.
The buyer is already in the room: Reddit threads like the $6K parent overpayment and the 61-year-old husband being billed for his father's 1980 benefit show adult children and spouses doing the legwork today, with no done-for-you option to hand them.
The gap is a canyon, not a crack: the market jumps from free SSA phone lines and 24help.org's guided form straight to $3,000 attorney retainers, with nothing at the $500-$1,500 flat fee a family would actually swipe for.

REASONS TO NOT BUILD

Family-pays conversion is the one leg nobody has tested: Reddit proves adult children do the legwork, but it does not prove they will wire $900 to fight a federal benefits case for a parent, so the first 20 sales are the real experiment.
SSA representative rules are a compliance minefield: to charge a fee for representing a claimant before SSA you generally need accreditation and fee approval, and a pure form-prep service lives in a gray zone that varies by state UPL rules.
Nobody is searching for this solution yet: 4,400 people a month search the problem but only 390 search for an overpayment attorney, so paid acquisition is expensive and distribution is a grind through Reddit comments and legal-aid partnerships one case at a time.
Policy whiplash can kill the urgency overnight: a reversal of the 50% default back to 10%, or a congressional waiver amnesty, would soften the acute pain that makes families open their wallets.

First up.

Search demand is for the problem, not for this solution. Google Ads shows 4,400 US searches a month for "social security overpayment" and 1,600 for "ssa-632," but only 390 for "social security overpayment attorney" at a $10.31 CPC. Nobody is typing "social security clawback service" because the category does not exist in people's heads yet. Ads are the wrong first move: the attorney-term CPC is high, and the problem-term clicks will not convert cold because the visitor does not yet trust a non-attorney, flat-fee product. The first channel is presence in the rooms where families already ask for help.

THE VERDICT

Should you build this?

REASONS TO BUILD

The policy clock is on your side: SSA switched to 50% default withholding on April 25, 2025, which means every new notice issued since is five times more painful than it was in 2024.
The attorney door is provably closed: a vision-impaired mom with a $34K overpayment wrote that no attorney would help, and SSA fee rules structurally prevent contingency work on waivers, so there is no incumbent fighting for your lane.
The buyer is already in the room: Reddit threads like the $6K parent overpayment and the 61-year-old husband being billed for his father's 1980 benefit show adult children and spouses doing the legwork today, with no done-for-you option to hand them.
The gap is a canyon, not a crack: the market jumps from free SSA phone lines and 24help.org's guided form straight to $3,000 attorney retainers, with nothing at the $500-$1,500 flat fee a family would actually swipe for.

REASONS TO NOT BUILD

Family-pays conversion is the one leg nobody has tested: Reddit proves adult children do the legwork, but it does not prove they will wire $900 to fight a federal benefits case for a parent, so the first 20 sales are the real experiment.
SSA representative rules are a compliance minefield: to charge a fee for representing a claimant before SSA you generally need accreditation and fee approval, and a pure form-prep service lives in a gray zone that varies by state UPL rules.
Nobody is searching for this solution yet: 4,400 people a month search the problem but only 390 search for an overpayment attorney, so paid acquisition is expensive and distribution is a grind through Reddit comments and legal-aid partnerships one case at a time.
Policy whiplash can kill the urgency overnight: a reversal of the 50% default back to 10%, or a congressional waiver amnesty, would soften the acute pain that makes families open their wallets.
